text: Lectures 7 to 12 answer one question: how do we get a big gain and a big output swing at the same time?
Every scene says why we do something before how. Orange your turn stops wait for your answer.
Lecture 3 to 6 built one-stage op amps. The telescopic cascode has a huge gain, about g M r O, squared over 2 about 1250 with G M R O equals 50.
Read the tower: one block per transistor, its height equals the voltage across it. Every block needs at least its V overdrive (0.2 volts).
Push V out up: the block above it (M 6) shrinks until it is squeezed to 0.2 volts. That is the ceiling, 1.4 volts.
Pull V out down: now M 4 is squeezed, at 0.6 volts. Five blocks of 0.2 volts leave only 0.8 volts of the 1.8 volts for the output.
So the question of Lecture 7: can we keep the big gain and still let the output swing nearly rail to rail?
Answer: give the two jobs to two different stages. One makes the gain, the other makes the swing.
More cascodes: more gain, less swing. Two stages split the jobs.
Strip any amplifier down to its core. An input transistor turns the input voltage into a current,
a small-signal current G M V in. Then that current has to go somewhere: into the output node.
Seen from the output, every amplifier is this: a current G M V in pushed into the resistance R out at the output node.
So the gain is always G M times R out. Keep this line: it explains everything in Lectures 7 to 9.
A stage is exactly that: one input device and one high-resistance node. Each such node also carries a capacitance, so it makes one pole (it slows the amplifier down).
The 5-T O T A, the telescopic and the folded cascode were all one stage. Now we chain two of them.
A stage is one input device and its load: A equals G M R out; stages multiply.
Meet circuit 1 by its currents first. Numbers from Tutorial 3 Q 2: a 1 milliamp tail, and 1 milliamp in each stage-2 branch. Current always runs from V D D down to ground.
Start at the source. The tail M 9 is a current sink: it pulls I S S equals 1 milliamp out of node P and sends it to ground. In an N mos the current runs drain to source: downwards.
Where does that 1 milliamp come from? Only two wires reach P: one through M 1, one through M 2. K C L at P: I S S equals I D 1 plus I D 2. Equal inputs share it equally: 0.5 milliamps each.

Each half comes down from V D D through a P mos load: M 3 feeds M 1, M 4 feeds M 2. In a P mos the current runs source to drain, so it also flows downwards. The sources set the current; the devices only share it.
Stage 2 has its own current, set by its own sinks M 7 and M 8: 1 milliamp from V D D through M 5, past V out 1, down through M 7. The same on the right with M 6 and M 8.
What flows from X into M 5? Nothing: X only touches M 5’s gate, and a gate draws no current. The stages pass a voltage (X sets M 5’s V G S ), never a current.
Now a small differential input. M 1 carries delta I more, M 2 delta I less. The tail total stays 1 milliamp: what one side gains, the other side loses.
M 3 and M 4 do not change, so M 1’s extra delta I is pulled out of node X and X falls, while Y gets delta I extra and rises. Those voltage swings are the signal that stage 2 amplifies.
The current rules of circuit 1 on one card. Next, the same circuit read for gain.
Your first circuit. In the middle: a differential pair M 1, M 2 with P mos current-source loads M 3, M 4 and tail M 9, the familiar one-stage amplifier.
That middle part is stage 1 (your red loop). Its outputs are nodes X and Y.
Its gain: the pair’s G M times the resistance at X, which is R O 1 looking down in parallel with R O 3 looking up.
Now the new part (green loops). X drives the gate of M 5, a P mos common-source device with an N mos current source M 7 below it. Same on the right with M 6, M 8.
That is stage 2: one transistor and one current source between the rails. Its output is V out 1 (and V out 2 ).
Stage 2’s gain is read the same way: G M 5 times R O 5 in parallel with R O 7. Only about G M R O over 2, modest.
Two stages in a chain: stage 1 amplifies by Ay 1, then stage 2 amplifies that again by Ay 2. Gains multiply: A equals Ay 1 Ay 2.
Follow a signal: a tiny V in becomes Ay 1 V in at X, which is M 5’s gate, and stage 2 multiplies it again at V out 1.
With G M R O equals 50 each stage gives about 25, so the whole op amp gives about 625, and the output still sits in a two-device column.
Why this matters: the gain came from multiplying stages, not from stacking devices in the output column.
A equals Ay 1 Ay 2: stage 1 gives gain, stage 2 gives swing.
Ay 2 equals G M 5, 6 ( R O 5, 6 in parallel with R O 7, 8 ).
Same 1.8 volts supply, same 0.2 volts per block. The telescopic output column holds five blocks: only 0.8 volts is left for the output.
Stage 2 is a common-source stage: two blocks, one device to each rail. Its output can swing 1.4 volts, from 0.2 volts to 1.6 volts.
That is the whole trick: the output that has to swing far sits in a short column, so it gets almost the full supply.
Your page draws it as two blocks: a high-gain amplifier followed by a high-swing amplifier.
Why this order? The big signal only exists at the final output. Stage 1’s output moves by just V out over Ay 2, a few millivolts,
so stage 1 can afford a tall, cramped stack of cascodes (lots of gain, little room). Stage 2 gets the short column because it must make the big swing.
Swap them, and the cramped stage would have to make the big swing, exactly what we were trying to avoid.
A CS stage has two blocks per column: the output swings to within V overdrive of each rail.
Circuit 2 is a telescopic first stage and a common-source second stage. Follow its currents with the Tutorial 3 Q 3 numbers: a 1 milliamp tail, 0.5 milliamps in each stage-2 branch.
Start at the tail source: it pulls I S S equals 1 milliamp out of node P, down to ground.
Only two wires reach P. K C L at P: I S S equals I D 1 plus I D 2, so with equal inputs each side carries 0.5 milliamps.

Now follow the left side upwards: M 1’s 0.5 milliamps comes through M 3, which gets it through M 5, which gets it from M 7. A telescopic column has no side exit: one current through four devices in series.
Directions: in the P mos M 7 and M 5 the current runs source to drain, in the N mos M 3 and M 1 drain to source. Both are downwards, from V D D to ground.
Stage 2 runs its own 0.5 milliamps per side, set by the sinks M 11 and M 12, through M 9 and M 10. X only touches M 9’s gate, so no current crosses from stage 1 to stage 2.
Right: one current per column. In a telescopic stage the current can leave a column only at P.
A small differential input: M 1 takes delta I more, M 2 delta I less, the total stays 1 milliamp. The cascode M 3 passes M 1’s change straight up to X: the same current in as out.
But M 5 and M 7 above X are fixed sources, so the extra delta I comes out of node X: X falls and Y rises. That is stage 1’s output signal, which M 9 and M 10 then amplify.
The current rules of circuit 2. Next, the same circuit read for gain.
Your second circuit. The middle is now a full telescopic cascode (M 1, M 8): input pair, N mos cascodes M 3, M 4, P mos cascodes M 5, M 6 and P mos sources M 7, M 8.
Stage 1’s outputs X and Y drive the gates of M 9, M 10: P mos common-source devices loaded by N mos current sources M 11, M 12. That is stage 2.
Gain of stage 1, the usual two looks from X: looking up you see the P mos cascode, G M 5 R O 5 R O 7,
looking down you see the N mos cascode, G M 3 R O 3 R O 1. The input current G M 1 V in meets the two in parallel.
Stage 2 is read the same way: Ay 2 equals G M 9 ( R O 9 in parallel with R O 11 ). With G M R O equals 50: Ay 1 about 1250, Ay 2 about 25, so A about 31 000.
A detail the tutorials ask (Tutorial 3 Q 2, Q 3): what DC voltage sits at X? X is M 9’s gate, and M 9’s source is V D D.
M 9 carries a fixed current, so its V G S 9 is fixed. That is a link: X equals V D D minus V G S 9. Stage 2 decides where stage 1’s output sits.
Then check stage 1 still fits at that level: the devices between X and the rails must each keep their V overdrive block.
Next: what does chaining two high-resistance nodes cost us?
Ay 1 equals G M 1 G M 5 R O 5 R O 7 in parallel with G M 3 R O 3 R O 1, Ay 2 equals G M 9 ( R O 9 in parallel with R O 11 ).
Level between the stages is a link: X equals V D D minus V G S 9.
Your page sketches two Bode plots. Gain in dB against frequency.
One stage: one high-resistance node, so one pole. Past it the gain falls at 20 decibels per decade, and the phase lag stops at 90 degrees.
Two stages: X and V out are both high-resistance nodes, each with its capacitance. The DC gain is higher, but there are two poles: minus 20, then minus 40 decibels over decade.
Why it matters: each pole adds up to 90 degrees of lag. With two, the lag heads to 180 degrees before the gain drops to 1, inside a feedback loop that rings or oscillates.
So two-stage op amps always need compensation (Lecture 17). For now remember: more gain and more swing, paid for with a second pole.
Two stages means two poles, so the op amp needs compensation.
Circuit 3 is circuit 2 with one output. Stage 1 is unchanged: the tail’s 1 milliamp splits at P into 0.5 milliamps per column.
Stage 2, left: M 9 sends its 0.5 milliamps down into M 11. M 11 is a diode (gate tied to drain), so it turns that current into a gate voltage.
M 12 shares M 11’s gate and source, so it copies the current: 0.5 milliamps pulled down out of the output node. The mirror sets the right branch; the gate wire itself carries nothing.
From above, M 10 pushes its 0.5 milliamps into the output node. K C L at V out: 0.5 milliamps in from M 10, 0.5 milliamps out through M 12. Balanced, so V out sits still.
The halves add: 2i leaves the output node, so V out falls. One output, but nothing of the signal is wasted.
The current rules of the mirror version. Next, the same idea in the signal picture.
Same op amp, but now we want one output instead of two.
M 11 becomes a diode (gate tied to drain) and M 12 shares its gate: a current mirror, exactly as in the 5-T O T A.
Follow a signal. The left CS device M 9 carries plus i more; that current goes into the diode M 11,
and M 12 copies it, pulling plus i more out of the output. Meanwhile M 10, driven the opposite way, pushes i less in.
Both changes move V out the same way: the two halves add. One output, full differential gain, nothing wasted.
Remember the mirror’s job in one line: the diode turns a current into a gate voltage, the mirror copies it to the other side, and the halves add.
Single output: diode M 11 and mirror M 12, the two halves add.
A new idea to get gain. Start from the one line you know: Ay V equals G M times R out.
G M is the input device’s G M equals 2 I D over V overdrive. More of it needs more current (power) or a smaller overdrive: your page says very hard to improve.
R out is different, your page says needs to be improved. We already know one way: stack cascodes.
Your page’s stack: looking into M 1’s drain you see R O 1,
put M 2 on top and it multiplies that by G M 2 R O 2 (up multiplies),
add M 3 and it multiplies again: G M 3 R O 3 G M 2 R O 2 R O 1. Each cascode gives another factor of about 50.
But each stacked cascode adds another V overdrive block to the output column, the swing problem again.
So Razavi asks: can we get that multiplication of R out without stacking another device? That is gain boosting.
Your page tries two ways. The first fails, and seeing why it fails makes the second one obvious.
Ay V equals G M times R out: G M is hard to raise, so raise R out without stacking.
The obvious idea: put an amplifier Ay 1 in front of the gate. The transistor now sees Ay 1 V in,
so I out over V in equals Ay 1 G M. It looks as if G M went up by Ay 1!
Now be honest about the transistor: it has its own R O 2, and below its source sits a resistance R S (in a cascode that is the input device’s R O ).
The gate sees Ay 1 V in, but the source has risen by I out R S. The current source inside M 2 gives G M 2 times V G S.
Part of that current leaks back through R O 2: a current divider leaves I O R O 2 over ( R O 2 plus R S ) at the output.
Put the first line into the second and collect every I out on the left.
Solve. This is your page’s last line.
Read it carefully: it is Ay 1 times the plain degenerated transistor, about 1 over R S. The transistor did not get any better.
Ay 1 is just an extra amplifier in front, a separate stage. And R out at the output is unchanged. Your page’s verdict: No improvement.
Lesson: boosting the input side is the wrong place. The amplifier must fight the output resistance instead.
An amplifier in front of the gate gives no improvement.
First recall a plain device with R S under its source (your page): looking into its drain you see R S plus R O plus G M R S R O, the cascode formula.
Now the working idea: an amplifier Ay 1 watches the source (its minus input) and drives the gate. To find R out, kill the input and push a test voltage V X into the drain.
A current I X flows in. Everything is about how hard M 2 fights it.
I X through R S lifts the source by I X R S. A plain device’s V G S would shrink by just that much.
But the amplifier sees the source rise and drives the gate down by Ay 1 I X R S (your page: minus Ay 1 I X R S ).
So V G S shrinks by (1 plus Ay 1 ) I X R S: M 2 fights back (1 plus Ay 1 ) times harder. The drain looks (1 plus Ay 1 ) times stiffer.
The algebra on your page: the current source inside M 2 is G M 2 times V G S, which is -(1 plus Ay 1 ) I X R S.
K C L at the drain: I X is that current plus what flows through R O 2, which sees V X minus I X R S.
Solve for V X over I X: R out equals R S plus R O 2 plus G M 2 (1 plus Ay 1 ) R S R O 2, the cascode result with its big term multiplied by (1 plus Ay 1 ).
With G M R O equals 50 and Ay 1 equals 50 that is 51 times more output resistance, and nothing new was stacked in the output column. That is gain boosting.
Remember the picture: the amplifier holds the source still by moving the gate the opposite way.
R out equals R S plus R O plus (1 plus Ay 1 ) G M R S R O.

Now look up, into a source (your page, right): a plain device with R D on its drain shows ( R D plus R O ) over (1 plus G M R O ), about 1 over G M, small. Down divides.
Boost it: the amplifier again moves the gate against any change of the source, so the device fights (1 plus Ay 1 ) times harder,
and the source looks (1 plus Ay 1 ) times stiffer: ( R D plus R O ) over (1 plus (1 plus Ay 1 ) G M R O ).
One rule for both directions: up multiplies, down divides, and boosting puts an extra (1 plus Ay 1 ) into both.
Why we need the second one: in a boosted cascode, the input device’s current has to choose between going up into that stiff source or down into R O 1. Next scene.
Down into a boosted drain: R S plus R O plus (1 plus Ay 1 ) G M R S R O.
Up into a boosted source: ( R D plus R O ) over (1 plus (1 plus Ay 1 ) G M R O ).

Small-signal picture at X: M 1 pushes G M 1 V in into the node, which has two exits, up into M 2’s boosted source, or down through R O 1.
With 1 over G M 2 equals 1 kilo-ohm and Ay 1 equals 50 the up path is about 20 ohms; R O 1 is tens of k ohms. Current takes the easy path: almost all of it goes up.
The little box on your page is the current divider: the current into R 2 is I R 1 over ( R 1 plus R 2 ), the other resistance on top.
Here: I out equals G M 1 V in R O 1 over ( R O 1 plus 1 over ((1 plus Ay 1 ) G M 2 )) about G M 1 V in.

Before the booster’s maths, follow its currents. Two columns hang from V D D: the output column ( I 1, M 2, M 1) and the booster column ( I 2, M 3).
The direction rule: current flows down from V D D to ground. An N mos takes it in at the drain and lets it out at the source. The current sources decide how much.
The booster column: I 2 pushes its current down into M 3’s drain, and M 3 sinks all of it to ground. With the 2025 mid sem numbers that is 100 microamps.
That node also feeds M 2’s gate, and X feeds M 3’s gate, but gates draw no current. Nothing crosses between the columns: they are two separate loops.
The output column is one series string: I 1, then M 2, then M 1. The same current all the way down: I D 2 equals I D 1 equals I 1.
Watch the names: your Lecture 8 page calls the output source I 1, but the 2025 mid sem and Tutorial 4 call it I 2, and I 1 is M 3’s load there. Follow the branch, not the letter.
With a signal, the sources still hold the currents. If X rises, M 3 wants more than I 2 can give, so its drain, M 2’s gate, falls instead. The currents stay put; the voltages move.
Remember: two columns flowing down, series devices share one current, and gates carry none. Now the same circuit, with its gain.
Implementation 1. The booster is just M 3: its gate sits on X (M 2’s source), its drain drives M 2’s gate, and I 2 is its load. A common-source amplifier.
Check the sign: if X rises, M 3 conducts more and pulls its drain, M 2’s gate, down. Exactly the opposite way the booster must push.
Its gain is G M 3 R O 3, so the whole gain is G M 1 (1 plus G M 3 R O 3 ) G M 2 R O 2 R O 1, your page’s line.
The cost (green note on your page): in a plain cascode, X only needs M 1’s check: V overdrive 1, 0.2 volts.
But now X is M 3’s gate, and M 3’s source is ground. That is a link: X must sit a whole V G S 3 (0.7 volts) up, minimum voltage equals V G S 3 and not V overdrive 1.
M 2’s check then puts the output at least V overdrive 2 above X: V out, min equals V G S 3 plus V overdrive 2 equals 0.9 volts instead of 0.4 volts. Disadvantage: one V threshold of swing lost.
Also notice (Tutorial 4 Q 1 a): M 2’s gate is two links above ground, V G 2 equals V G S 3 plus V G S 2.
Can a P mos booster avoid the V G S 3 penalty? That is implementation 2.

X sits at V G S 3, so V out, min equals V G S 3 plus V overdrive 2.
Implementation 2’s currents. The output column is the same as before. The booster is now a P mos, M 3, hanging from V D D, with the sink I 2 under it.
Direction rule for a P mos: its source is on top, at V D D. Current goes in at the source and out at the drain, still downward.
So the booster current runs from V D D, in at M 3’s source, out at its drain G, and down through I 2: I D 3 equals I 2.
The output column: I 1 flows down through M 2 and then M 1. Same current in each, they are in series.
K C L at P: M 2 brings I 1 in, M 1 takes it out, and M 3’s gate takes nothing. The booster and the output column never exchange current.

Implementation 2: make the booster a P mos CS stage. M 3’s source is at V D D, its gate on P (M 2’s source), its drain G drives M 2’s gate, I 2 below.
Now check if M 3 can stay saturated. Use the P mos fence: its drain may be at most V threshold 3 above its gate.
M 3’s drain is G, its gate is P: V G is at most V P plus V threshold 3.
But G is M 2’s gate and P is M 2’s source, a link: V G equals V P plus V G S 2.
Substitute.
Cancel V P: M 2’s V G S must stay below one threshold.
Your page’s little cross-section shows what that means: with V G S 2 near threshold, M 2’s channel is barely formed. M 2 would need a huge width to carry its current.
So implementation 2 fails, not because of the gain, but because of a fence. Implementation 3 keeps the P mos input and fixes the level problem by folding.
P mos booster: V G S 2 is at most V threshold 3, M 2 is barely on. It fails.
The folded booster has three current paths. Follow them one at a time: the output column, the I 3 column through M 4, and the P mos M 3.
Output column first: I 1 flows down through M 2 and M 1. Nothing else joins it, M 2’s gate and M 3’s gate draw no current.
Second path: I 3 pushes its current down into M 4’s drain. The wire to M 2’s gate takes nothing, so all of I 3 goes through M 4 and arrives at node F, M 4’s source.

Third path, the fold: the P mos M 3 takes current from its own little V D D rail, in at its source, out at its drain, and the wire brings it round and up to node F. It turns back on itself: that is the fold.
K C L at F: I 3 and M 3’s current both arrive, and I 2 takes the sum to ground. So I D 3 equals I 2 minus I 3: with 150 and 50 microamps, M 3 carries 100 microamps.
Now the signal. X rises, so the P mos M 3’s gate goes up and M 3 carries a little less: minus delta I. But I 2 and I 3 are fixed sources.
M 3 gives delta I less, so M 4 must take delta I more, the total into I 2 stays fixed. I 3 can’t supply it, so M 2’s gate is pulled down: X up, gate down.
The rule of the fold: the P mos branch and the M 4 branch share the bottom sink. Whatever one loses, the other gains; the total is always I 2.
Remember the fold: two branches share one sink, so whatever M 3 loses, M 4 gains. Now the booster’s gain.
Implementation 3 (bottom of your page): the P mos booster M 3 is folded into an N mos cascode M 4, with current sources I 3 (top) and I 2 (bottom).
M 3 senses M 2’s source with its gate. Its drain current is folded into M 4’s source; M 4 carries the signal up to its drain, which drives M 2’s gate.
The booster is itself a cascode amplifier: G M equals G M 3, and looking into M 4’s drain you see a cascode, G M 4 R O 4 R O 3. So Ay 1 equals G M 3 G M 4 R O 4 R O 3, about 2500 instead of 50.
Why it fixes implementation 1: a P mos input is happy with its gate near ground (Lecture 6), so X can stay just V overdrive 1 up. No V G S 3 penalty.
Best of both: no swing lost, and a booster gain of g M r O, squared instead of G M R O. This is the version Tutorial 4 Q 3 and the 2024 mid sem Q 4 use.
Folded booster: Ay 1 equals G M 3 G M 4 R O 4 R O 3, no swing lost.

The Tutorial 5 Q 2 folded cascode. Two P mos sources at the top each push I P down from V D D into a folding node.
The input pair hangs from those nodes. The tail pulls I S S, and with equal inputs M 1 and M 2 each take I S S over 2, out of the left and the right folding node.
K C L at the left folding node: I P comes in, and leaves either through M 1 or down the cascode branch.

The rest, I P minus I S S over 2, folds down through the P mos cascode, the output node and the N mos cascode into M 3. M 3 must sink exactly that, and its gate is V E: the C M F B amplifier makes it match.

With a differential input each cascode branch changes opposite to its input transistor. M 3 and M 4 do not change, so the difference flows out of one output and into the other. The outputs move apart; the C M stays.
The current rules for the folded cascode: the top source current folds, part into the input pair and the rest down the cascode, and the C M F B sets the bottom sinks to match.

Let us follow the current in Lecture 11’s telescopic, with the numbers of Tutorial 5 Question 1: each column carries half a milliamp.

Start at the top. M 8 and M 9 have a fixed gate bias, so they are current sources: each pushes half a milliamp down its own column. A P mos conducts from its source at the supply to its drain, so the current flows down.
Nothing leaves the column on the way down. The same current passes the output node, then the N mos cascode and the input device. An N mos conducts from drain to source: down again.
The blue wires from the outputs to the gates of M 10 and M 11 carry a voltage, not a current: a gate draws no current.
At node P the two columns meet. Kirchhoff’s current law: whatever flows into P must flow out, and the only way out is down through the triode devices M 10 and M 11.
One milliamp arrives at P. With equal outputs, M 10 and M 11 are equal resistors, so they split it equally: half a milliamp each, down to ground.
Now add a small differential input: the input device M 2 takes a little more, I D plus delta I, and M 3 a little less, I D minus delta I.
Add them at P: plus delta I and minus delta I cancel. The total stays at one milliamp; the input only moves current from one side to the other.

But the P mos source on top still gives exactly I D. The extra delta I on the left has to come out of the output node, so V out 1 falls, and on the right V out 2 rises. That current mismatch is the output signal.
And the tail? V out 1 down makes M 10 a bigger resistor, V out 2 up makes M 11 a smaller one: the split under P shifts, but the sum still matches one milliamp.
Your page’s circuit: a telescopic op amp whose tail is two transistors M 10, M 11 in deep triode, with their gates driven by the two outputs.
They sit between node P and ground with only a tiny V D S (= V P ), so each is a resistor set by its gate, that is, by an output voltage.
In parallel, conductances add: 1 over R total equals 1 over R on 10 plus 1 over R on 11,
each conductance is mu n C O X W over L ( V G S minus V threshold ) with V G S equals an output,
so only the sum V out 1 plus V out 2 appears, twice the output C M.
Watch the conductances. A differential signal raises one output and lowers the other: G10 grows, G11 shrinks by the same amount, the total does not move. The sensor ignores the signal.
A common-mode rise raises both: the total conductance grows, R total falls, the tail pulls harder, and the outputs are pulled back down. Feedback, built right into the tail.
R total equals 1 over ( mu n C O X W over L ( V out 1 plus V out 2 minus 2 V threshold )): sees C M, blind to D M.
Follow the current in the pair sensor. Two sources set everything: M 5 at the top, and the two sinks I 1 at the bottom. Take M 5 as 20 microamps and each sink as 50.
M 5 is a P mos with a fixed gate bias: a current source. Its 20 microamps flow down from the supply, source to drain, into the node below it.
At that node it splits: part goes down through M 3, the rest through M 4. K C L: I 5 equals I D 3 plus I D 4. With equal outputs the circuit is symmetric, so the halves are equal.
Each follower carries its own current from the supply, drain to source. At the follower’s source node it meets M 3’s current, and the sink below takes both: I 1 equals I D 1 plus I D 3.
M 3 gets 10 microamps, so the follower M 1 carries the rest of the sink: 50 minus 10, 40 microamps. The same on the right.
The rule for every node: the sources set the currents, the devices only share them. If M 3 takes more, M 1 must take less, because the sink below is fixed.
Another sensor on your page: followers M 1, M 2 copy the outputs, and P mos devices M 3, M 4 (gates at V R E F ) compare them, sharing the current source M 5.
Each device’s current follows the square law of its own difference from V R E F, so the sensed current is a sum of squares (your page’s last line).
And a sum of squares does not depend only on the sum of the outputs: for big swings the differential signal leaks into the reading. Good for small swings only.
